evidence.text: Look for. • Category selection mechanics: Target existing, massive categories so you do not have to educate the consumer on what the product is. Look for a "sea of sameness" where all incumbents look identical (e.g., all dish soaps are green and toxic; all vitamins are round and pseudo-scientific). • Cultural shift mapping: Identify a macro trend happening elsewhere (e.g., "boutique fitness as a spiritual pursuit") and apply it to the stagnant category (e.g., daily vitamins) to create "creative tension." • Cross-industry theft mechanics: Steal aesthetics from completely unrelated industries. The further apart the dots, the more powerful the idea (e.g., stealing high-end houseware vase shapes and applying them to dish soap packaging). • The "One Iteration" Rule: Change exactly ONE major variable from the core product expectation. If you change two or three things simultaneously, the product becomes "too novel," breaking consumer adoption. • Naming constraints: The holy grail of brand naming is one word, four letters. Identify a core "jumping-off word" based on the product's ultimate goal (e.g., "technique" for cleaning -> Method; "friendly" for vitamins -> Olly), and base the naming search purely on that feeling.

cards.title: Category Selection Mechanics
cards.claim: To avoid consumer education, target existing, massive categories; look for a 'sea of sameness' where incumbents look identical.
cards.action: Select an existing, massive product category containing incumbents that look identical, so consumer education is not required.
applies_when: Selecting a product category to enter
Searching for incumbent sameness in a category
do_not_use_when: No explicit do-not-use conditions are stated in the passage.
unknowns: Whether a sea of sameness is required or only desired
Whether avoiding consumer education is the only criterion
evidence_quotes: Target existing, massive categories so you do not have to educate the consumer on what the product is.
Look for a "sea of sameness" where all incumbents look identical

cards.title: One Iteration Rule for Product Novelty
cards.claim: Change exactly one major variable from the core product expectation; changing two or three simultaneously makes the product 'too novel' and breaks consumer adoption.
cards.action: Limit product changes to exactly one major variable from the core expectation.
applies_when: Testing consumer adoption for a novel product variation
do_not_use_when: Not specified in the passage beyond avoiding multiple simultaneous changes.
evidence_quotes: Change exactly ONE major variable from the core product expectation.
If you change two or three things simultaneously, the product becomes "too novel," breaking consumer adoption.

cards.title: Brand Naming Constraints and Jumping-Off Word
cards.claim: A naming ideal is one word, four letters; identify a core jumping-off word based on the product's ultimate goal and base the naming search purely on that feeling.
cards.action: Identify a jumping-off word from the product's ultimate goal and base the naming search on that feeling, aiming for a one-word, four-letter name.
applies_when: Deriving a name from the product's ultimate goal
unknowns: Whether one word and four letters are strict constraints or aspirational
How to choose the ultimate goal word
Whether trademark or linguistic checks constrain the result
evidence_quotes: The holy grail of brand naming is one word, four letters.
Identify a core "jumping-off word" based on the product's ultimate goal
base the naming search purely on that feeling.
